Potem, po kolei: - „Wiemy, że żaden prawdziwy alkoholik nigdy nie odzyskuje kontroli” (s. 30). Alkoholicy ich typu są „w szponach postępującej choroby” (s. 30). - „Jesteśmy jak ludzie, którzy stracili nogi; nowe nigdy im nie odrosną” (s. 30). Żadne leczenie nie sprawi, że alkoholicy ich rodzaju staną się tacy jak inni ludzie (s. 30–31). - Trzydziestoletni mężczyzna, pijący ciężkimi ciągami, postanowił nie tknąć ani kropli, dopóki nie zbije majątku i nie przejdzie na emeryturę. Przez „dwadzieścia pięć lat nie wziął do ust ani kropli” (s. 32), potem w wieku pięćdziesięciu pięciu lat przeszedł na emeryturę, pewien, że długa trzeźwość pozwala mu pić jak inni ludzie. W ciągu dwóch miesięcy trafił do szpitala. Nie potrafił ani kontrolować picia, ani go przerwać, i w ciągu czterech lat już nie żył (s. 32–33). - Lekcja: „Większość z nas wierzyła, że jeśli przez długi czas pozostaniemy trzeźwi, będziemy potem mogli pić normalnie” (s. 33). Jeśli więc planujemy przestać, „nie może być żadnych zastrzeżeń ani żadnej czającej się myśli, że kiedyś staniemy się odporni na alkohol” (s. 33).

Czytane w ten sposób „raz alkoholik, zawsze alkoholik” i „wyzdrowieli” nie są ze sobą sprzeczne: jedno dotyczy tego, czy kiedykolwiek możesz znów bezpiecznie pić, drugie tego, czy problem picia został rozwiązany.

Te pojęcia były też własnymi pojęciami Grupy Oksfordzkiej i w oczach opinii publicznej wiązałyby z nią AA. - Większość alkoholików chciała być anonimowa, podczas gdy Grupy Oksfordzkie „w dużym stopniu opierały się na używaniu znanych nazwisk” (Anonimowi Alkoholicy wkraczają w dojrzałość, 1957).

555c3c02e786: <0>Rozdział 2, „Jest rozwiązanie” (1939).</0> Książka przedstawia swój plan: rozdziały wyjaśniające alkoholizm i zwracające się do agnostyka, a potem: „Dalej podane są jasne wskazówki pokazujące, jak wyzdrowieliśmy. Po nich następują czterdzieści dwa osobiste doświadczenia.” (s. 29). Historie, jak mówi, „dają rzetelny przekrój naszej Wspólnoty” (s. 29) i pokazują, co naprawdę wydarzyło się w życiu autorów. Ich celem jest utożsamienie się: autorzy wierzą, że tylko odsłaniając siebie, sprawią, że czytelnicy „dadzą się przekonać i powiedzą: «Tak, ja też jestem jednym z nich; muszę to mieć»” (s. 29).
3a1dfa85480b: <0>Rozdział 4, „My, agnostycy” (1939).</0> To w historiach książka pokazuje, jak różnie członkowie rozumieją Boga: „W naszych historiach osobistych znajdziesz wielką różnorodność sposobów, w jakie każdy z opowiadających podchodzi do Siły większej od niego samego i jak ją pojmuje.” (s. 50). 27e39e19e8ab: <0>Rozdział 5, „Jak to działa” (1939).</0> Rozdział przechodzi od historii do programu: „Nasze historie pokazują w ogólnych zarysach, jacy kiedyś byliśmy, co się stało i jacy jesteśmy obecnie.” (s. 58). d54ed5205d99: <0>Sama część z historiami.</0> Jej strona tytułowa mówi, że historie pokazują, „jak czterdziestu dwóch alkoholików wyzdrowiało ze swojej choroby” (s. 165), a każda część ma własny cel: część I pokazuje, „że trzeźwość w AA może być trwała”, część II może pomóc czytelnikowi rozstrzygnąć, czy jest alkoholikiem i czy AA jest dla niego, a część III daje nadzieję tym, którzy uważają swoje picie za beznadziejne (s. 167).

Głodu tego „nigdy nie wykorzeniono na stałe żadną znaną nam metodą leczenia” (s. xxx).

cbd2a73c0053: What they're sure of is the physical side itself. They write that "the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" (p. xxvi), and "any picture of the alcoholic which leaves out this physical factor is incomplete" (p. xxvi).
1a483ab8c23c: The allergy isn't the doctor's whole picture. Between drinks, he says, the alcoholic is "restless, irritable and discontented" (p. xxviii) until he can feel again the ease a few drinks bring. After the spree comes remorse and a firm resolution, repeated over and over (p. xxix). He doesn't think alcoholism is "entirely a problem of mental control" (p. xxix), but he also says there is very little hope "unless this person can experience an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).
57adaf3d3b8d: Chapter 2 says the same from the members' side. Once the alcoholic takes any alcohol, "something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense" (p. 22). But because the cycle can't start without the first drink, "the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23).

In the Big Book it turns up in members' stories. In "He Sold Himself Short" (Part I), the writer recalls being told that drinking was "a fatal illness made up of an allergy plus an obsession" (p. 261). In "It Might Have Been Worse" (Part II), the writer says the explanation of alcoholism as "an allergy of the body and an obsession of the mind" (p. 355) cleared up a lot for him. The 1939 chapters do speak of obsession in their own words: the idea that he will somehow control and enjoy his drinking "is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker" (p. 30).
78d5b03280a5: Bill W., writing in 1957, credits the pairing to Silkworth: "the obsession of the mind that compels us to drink and the allergy of the body that condemns us to go mad or die" (<0>A.A. The craving it describes starts with drinking, and the book pairs it with a mind that is "without defense against the first drink" (p. 24) and with Silkworth's own view that recovery takes a psychic change. 1f54ad750209: Look the quote up and read the whole passage it comes from: the whole chapter, the whole story or the whole talk. The Big Book is free on aa.org, so this takes minutes.
8675a9256553: Ask whether the rest of the passage points the same way as the quote. If the pages around it turn its meaning around, it has been taken out of context.
7cfa578d561b: Check who is speaking and when: the 1939 program text, a personal story, or a book written decades later.
59edd4f4b64a: The clearest example is the first line of Chapter 7, "Working With Others," which is often quoted to mean "help others to keep yourself sober." The chapter's other fourteen pages say the aim is the other alcoholic's life.
4ea739f27de3: The worked example: the first line of Chapter 7
4e0a28b1bd1c: <0>The line, read alone.</0> Chapter 7 opens: "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89). "It works when other activities fail." (p. 89). Lifted out by itself, that sounds like a reason to help others: it keeps <1>you</1> sober. Taught that way, Step Twelve becomes something you do for yourself.
8506d7dcd1da: <0>The same page.</0> Read to the bottom of p. 89 and the chapter has already named its subject, "Carry this message to other alcoholics!" (p. 89), and told you how to find drinkers who want to stop, through doctors, ministers and hospitals (p. 89). The page ends, after advising the reader to cooperate with doctors and ministers rather than criticize them: "To be helpful is our only aim." (p. 89).
b5ecc4a06e3b: <0>The whole chapter.</0> Read all fifteen pages (pp. 89–103) and the direction is plain: - The man you help is "under no obligation to you" (p. 94), and he's asked to "place the welfare of other people ahead of his own" (p. 94). - Don't stay too long with a man who isn't ready, because that "is to deny some other alcoholic an opportunity to live and be happy" (p. 96). - Expect the work to cost you nights' sleep, interruptions to your business, sharing your money and your home, and trips to courts, hospitals and jails (p. 97). - "Do not think of what you will get out of the occasion." (p. 102). "Think of what you can bring to it." (p. 102).
473170d16423: So the first line is true, and the book means it: the work does protect the helper. But it's a result, not the aim. Read whole, Chapter 7 is about rescuing the alcoholic who is still drinking. This page is laid out in full in <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>
2e61666bf397: <0>The same thing, said again in 1939.</0> Chapter 11 says the same about the first Akron members: "Though they knew they must help other alcoholics if they would remain sober, that motive became secondary." (Chapter 11, p. 159). "It was transcended by the happiness they found in giving themselves for others." (Chapter 11, p. 159). When a second passage in the same book confirms the reading of the whole, you can be more confident the lifted line was misleading.
0e589af9a0b6: In "Bill's Story," the phrase "Faith without works was dead, he said." (p. 14) is often quoted as a general saying. The sentence just before it tells you what "works" meant to the friend who said it: "Particularly was it imperative to work with others as he had worked with me." (p. 14). The next lines say that an alcoholic who didn't work for others would drink again (pp. 14–15). In context, the "works" are work with other alcoholics.

eb775820373b: What does "Rarely have we seen a person fail" really say, and who does it say may not recover?
7a9f82a67e06: It's the first sentence of Chapter 5, "How It Works." The book says that rarely "have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). It's a strong claim, but it has a condition: it's about people who follow the path thoroughly.
e96513c98fb3: The same paragraph names who may not recover: people who "cannot or will not completely give themselves to this simple program" (p. 58). These are usually people "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (p. 58), and some with "grave emotional and mental disorders" (p. 58).
ac8c850f8510: It doesn't blame them. Of the first group it says "They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way." (p. 58) Their chances are "less than average" (p. 58), which is not the same as none. Of the second group, "many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest" (p. 58).
e0bf03498f7c: Read in place, the paragraph turns on honesty. Right after the Steps, the book says no one has managed "anything like perfect adherence to these principles" (p. 60), so "thoroughly" doesn't mean perfectly.
aed804349492: Quoted by itself, the first sentence can be heard two ways. One is as a guarantee: follow the path and you won't fail. The other turns it around into a verdict on anyone who doesn't recover: he must not have followed it thoroughly. Neither reading can be checked against the sentence alone. It needs the rest of its paragraph.
866a8883d29c: The opening paragraph of Chapter 5 is short. In order, it says:
d5ef1e5b3af1: <0>The claim.</0> Rarely "have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). The word is "rarely," not "never."
0b7284ba1f5a: <0>Who doesn't recover.</0> Those who "cannot or will not" give themselves completely to the program (p. 58). The paragraph names both: "will not" is a refusal, "cannot" is an inability.
e63b9c66e938: <0>The usual reason.</0> Most are "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (p. 58). The book goes on: "There are such unfortunates." (p. 58) "They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way." (p. 58) They can't grasp and develop a way of living "which demands rigorous honesty" (p. 58). And: "Their chances are less than average." (p. 58)
c3ac9433cd08: <0>A second group.</0> "There are those, too, who suffer from grave emotional and mental disorders" (p. 58), and "many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest" (p. 58).
75901aac3ca0: So the paragraph names two conditions for recovery: giving oneself completely to "this simple program," and the capacity to be honest. Where people fall short of the second, it calls them unfortunate, not guilty.
d844bad8ad1e: The "path" isn't left vague. The paragraph itself calls it "this simple program" (p. 58), and the next page introduces the Twelve Steps as "suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59). In between, the book says what it asks of the reader. If you want what the members have and are willing to go to any length for it, "then you are ready to take certain steps" (p. 58). "At some of these we balked." (p. 58) And it begs the reader "to be fearless and thorough from the very start" (p. 58).
a1851cde3c2e: Then, right after the Steps, the book heads off the idea that "thoroughly" means flawlessly. "No one among us has been able to maintain anything like perfect adherence to these principles." (p. 60) "We are not saints." (p. 60) "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection." (p. 60)
a8990b35c484: <0>As a guarantee:</0> the book does mean the claim, and repeats its call for thoroughness. But it says "rarely," and the condition is following the path thoroughly. The same chapter says nobody follows it perfectly.
fc31ad7ab055: <0>As a verdict on those who don't recover:</0> the paragraph won't carry it. Its own explanation includes people who "cannot," who are "not at fault," and whose chances are lower but not gone. It describes people who are incapable of being honest with themselves, and it calls them unfortunates. It doesn't talk about relapse at all.
c27d73f75333: <0>The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955)</0> gives A.A.'s own figures as they stood then. Of alcoholics "who came to A.A. and really tried" (p. xx), half got sober at once and stayed that way, a quarter sobered up "after some relapses," and of the rest, those who stayed on showed improvement (p. xx). So by 1955 the book itself counted people who really tried and still relapsed before they recovered.
406e64a73100: <0><1>Pass It On</1> (1984)</0>, a biography of Bill W., says he wrote this paragraph when he wrote the Steps, and that an earlier manuscript said "directions" where the book now says "path." It also tells a story that Bill later wanted to change "rarely" to "never." The book calls that story apocryphal: "Bill himself said he never considered that change." (Pass It On, 1984)

50323fbe04e0: Mostly the Bible. Dr. Bob said in 1948 that the older members found three parts "absolutely essential": the Sermon on the Mount, the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians, and the Book of James (P-53).
7803734aee47: In Akron, members' recollections gathered in 1980 add three small books that were passed around by 1938–39, while the Big Book was being written: <0>The Upper Room</0> (a Methodist booklet of daily readings), Emmet Fox's <1>The Sermon on the Mount</1>, and Henry Drummond's <2>The Greatest Thing in the World</2>.
2fa8156ffe0c: That reading came with the Oxford Group's morning "quiet time." The program itself was passed on by word of mouth. A member's story describing Akron in 1937 says there was "no literature except various religious pamphlets" (p. 262).
9d75d1544b35: The 1939 Big Book doesn't list any of these books. It says only that "There are many helpful books also" (p. 87) and sends the reader to a priest, minister or rabbi for suggestions.
47ca6c9b2f10: In his last major talk, recorded in Detroit in December 1948, Dr. Bob described the early days at Akron. Before he met Bill W., he had spent two and a half years with the Oxford Group, had "done an immense amount of reading they had recommended" (P-53), and had refreshed his memory of the Bible. None of it kept him sober; what Bill brought him was the idea of helping someone else (P-53).
130a53c494ec: Of the time when he and Bill began working with Bill D., A.A. number three, in June 1935, he said: "we had no Twelve Steps, either; we had no Traditions" (P-53). "But we were convinced that the answer to our problems was in the Good Book." (P-53). Then the passage most often repeated: "To some of us older ones, the parts that we found absolutely essential were the Sermon on the Mount, the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians, and the Book of James." (P-53). He is talking about parts of the Bible here, not about a separate book.
cd8ab0f08077: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) both quote the same words (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980; Pass It On, 1984). The 1980 book adds: "They had the Bible, and they had the precepts of the Oxford Group." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
7a6d0e473756: When Bill lived with Dr. Bob and Anne Smith in the summer of 1935, the day began with the Oxford Group practice of a morning quiet time. Bill (1957) remembers Anne sitting by the fireplace to "read from the Bible, and then we would huddle together in stillness, awaiting inspiration and guidance" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The 1980 book quotes him: "James was our favorite" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and Anne would end with the verse "Faith without works is dead" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The Book of James was liked so well that some wanted to call the fellowship "The James Club" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). See <0>Is "faith without works is dead" in the Big Book?</0>
e2ba2684c304: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> gathers the recollections of early Akron members. They are memories recorded decades later, and the book itself notes how often they differ; as one member put it, they had all seen the same events "from different angles" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <1>The Bible first.</1> "The Bible was stressed as reading material, of course." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Patients in the hospital in the early days were allowed only a Bible to read (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <2><3>The Upper Room.</3></2> Dr. Bob's daughter, Sue, remembered that the morning Bible reading was later joined by <4>The Upper Room</4>, "a Methodist publication that provided a daily inspirational message" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Another early member, Dorothy S. M., called it "that little nickel book" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980) and said members were told to read it every morning (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). At the weekly meeting in T. Henry Williams's house, the leader usually took something from it, or from other literature, as a subject (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <5>Emmet Fox's <6>The Sermon on the Mount</6>.</5> Dorothy remembered it as "required reading for everybody" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), handed to men in the hospital as soon as they could focus their eyes. - <7>Henry Drummond's <8>The Greatest Thing in the World</8>.</7> Bob E. of Akron recalled it as another popular book of the time, which, like <9>The Upper Room</9>, was given out to members by a woman remembered as Mother G. (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
fcc811a345b4: Dorothy summed up: "Those were the three main books at the time" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), meaning Drummond, <0>The Upper Room</0> and Fox. Dr. Bob himself read widely: his son remembered that he read the Bible through three times and owned books from William James's <1>Varieties</1> to <2>For Sinners Only</2>, a book about the Oxford Group (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), but Dorothy said "he didn't push books at people" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
23d7a61b1992: A caution on dates: the 1980 book sets this reading in "1938-39" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), when the Big Book was being written, and it doesn't say when each of the three books first came into use. So our sources show they were read around the time the Big Book appeared, not that all three were in use from 1935.
730d340001a0: Frank Amos, soon to be one of A.A.'s first nonalcoholic trustees, looked into the Akron group for Mr. Rockefeller, and his report of February 1938 lists the practice: daily devotions, "a 'quiet time' of prayer and some reading from the Bible and other religious literature" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
5e9014f43110: The same book is plain about what was missing: "there was definitely a need for literature directed specifically to the alcoholic" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). That was the book, begun in 1938.

e94887fb8dbd: "Recovered" or "recovering": which word does the Big Book use?
b24eaafd8420: The Big Book's members call themselves "recovered." The 1939 Foreword opens with "more than one hundred men and women who have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii), and Chapter 2 says of the thousands they know, "Nearly all have recovered." (p. 17).
d5319ac825fa: The phrase "recovering alcoholic" is not in the fourth-edition Big Book. In our sources it appears in later books: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980), <1>Pass It On</1> (1984), P-16 (2018) and the current Service Manual.
a70cebafef5a: But "recovered" in the book doesn't mean cured or able to drink again. The same text says "We are not cured of alcoholism" and calls what members have "a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85).
39fee1ec1402: The book also uses "recovering" for someone in the process: the husband "who is recovering" (p. 122). The word isn't foreign to it; the self-description is "recovered."
8781e9901f71: The word runs through the book: - The Foreword to the First Edition: the members "have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii), and "To show other alcoholics precisely how we have recovered is the main purpose of this book." (p. xiii). - Dr. Silkworth's letter: "This man and over one hundred others appear to have recovered." (p. xxv). - Chapter 2: "Nearly all have recovered." (p. 17). "They have solved the drink problem." (p. 17). Readers are told the book will explain how "we have recovered from a hopeless condition of mind and body" (p. 20), followed by "clear-cut directions … showing how we recovered" (p. 29). - Chapter 7: the prospect's attention is drawn to the member "as a person who has recovered" (p. 90). - Chapter 9: "We have recovered, and have been given the power to help others." (p. 132). "We, who have recovered from serious drinking, are miracles of mental health." (p. 133). - Chapter 10: "An alcoholic who has recovered" can talk to another employee (p. 146).
a63d96f6a8fd: The fourth-edition title page reads "The Story of How Many Thousands of Men and Women Have Recovered from Alcoholism" (p. iii). Later A.A. writing keeps the word: in 1955 the Foreword to the Second Edition counted membership as "far above 150,000 recovered alcoholics" (p. xv), and <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) says that clergymen and physicians are the experts and "we, the recovered alcoholics, are their assistants" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).
c16314dd92b3: What "recovered" does and doesn't mean in the book
5421daafacd6: The book is careful about what has been recovered from: - Not from alcoholism as a condition. "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30). "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic." (p. 33). - Not once and for all. "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85). The reprieve is daily and depends on the member's spiritual condition (p. 85). Step Ten's work "should continue for our lifetime" (p. 84). - What members say they have recovered from is "a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii): the drink problem is solved (p. 17), so long as they keep in fit spiritual condition (p. 85).
904ab59fb5d0: The verb appears for someone in the middle of the process: - Chapter 9 opens by saying the members' "women folk have suggested certain attitudes a wife may take with the husband who is recovering" (p. 122). The chapter adds that "dad, though marvelously improved, is still convalescing" (p. 127). - Chapter 10: an employee who drinks "and is still trying to recover" will be honest about it (p. 146). - A later-edition footnote to Chapter 8 speaks of a woman alcoholic "whether she is still drinking or is recovering in A.A." (p. 104).
010a9a8a8881: What doesn't appear anywhere in the fourth-edition text, stories included, is the label "recovering alcoholic." "Recovered alcoholic(s)" appears in a few personal stories (pp. 273–274, 442).
27666e2ff955: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980): Dr. Bob's adult years "as an active and then as a recovering alcoholic" (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980).
40c7b7885230: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) uses "recovering alcoholics" in its narrative of the 1930s and early 1940s .
293aa292b198: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16, 2018): members may tell nonalcoholics "that we are recovering alcoholics" (P-16, 2018); GSO staff members "are themselves recovering alcoholics" (P-16, 2018).
d4e9ffd1160a: <0>The A.A. Service Manual</0> (2024–2026 edition): members in a home group "sustain connections with other recovering alcoholics."
7163a91aab5f: The 1939 text describes its members as recovered: rescued from a hopeless state, with the drink problem solved on a spiritual basis as a daily reprieve, and never able to drink safely again. "Recovering" as an identity is later usage. Neither the Big Book nor the later books in our sources say one word is right and the other wrong; this page only reports which word each source uses.

8c5978586f8d: The program text's fullest word on it is to a wife whose husband comes home drunk: "Though it is infinitely better that he have no relapse at all, as has been true with many of our men, it is by no means a bad thing in some cases." (p. 120). In those cases he sees that he must "redouble his spiritual activities if he expects to survive" (p. 120).
67e8d30922b2: So the text neither treats relapse as an expected stage nor writes off the person who drinks again. It treats drinking as deadly ("to drink is to die," p. 66), and it treats the man who slips and keeps trying with patience (pp. 120, 147).
8209f37a35fa: All our sources was searched for "part of recovery," "relapse," "slip" and their forms, with page breaks joined. "Part of recovery" turns up once, in a story where "Commitment and service were part of recovery" (p. 345). Nothing in any book says relapse is part of recovery.
8061ea455cb2: In the program text, "relapse" appears at pp. 26, 31, 35, 120 and 125. "Slip" meaning a drink appears at p. 100 ("We have seen others slip when the family came back too soon") and p. 139 (an executive who "did slip and was fired"). At p. 84 ("Self-seeking will slip away") and p. 110 (friends who "slipped away") it means something else.
7470d86a8cc6: <0>The danger.</0> Of the remedies they tried before A.A., the book says that in some instances there was "brief recovery, followed always by a still worse relapse" (p. 31). "Commencing to drink after a period of sobriety, we are in a short time as bad as ever." (p. 33). Chapter 3 is written to describe "the mental states that precede a relapse into drinking, for obviously this is the crux of the problem" (p. 35). Bill: if an alcoholic didn't work with others "he would surely drink again, and if he drank, he would surely die" (p. 15). "And with us, to drink is to die." (p. 66).
a9ada318c624: <0>Its causes.</0> Newcomers who kept certain facts to themselves: "Almost invariably they got drunk." (p. 73). Resentment brings it back (p. 66). Family quarrels and old affairs dug up again: "In most cases, the alcoholic survived this ordeal without relapse, but not always." (p. 125).
c9386b5acd74: <0>When it happens.</0> The passage that speaks most fully to a relapse in a man who has started the program is in "To Wives" (p. 120). Read in full, it says: - If you are satisfied he really wants to get over drinking, "you need not be alarmed" (p. 120). - "Though it is infinitely better that he have no relapse at all, as has been true with many of our men, it is by no means a bad thing in some cases." (p. 120). - He will see at once that he must "redouble his spiritual activities if he expects to survive" (p. 120). Don't remind him of his spiritual deficiency; "Cheer him up and ask him how you can be still more helpful." (p. 120). - "If he gets drunk, don't blame yourself." (p. 120). "God has either removed your husband's liquor problem or He has not. If not, it had better be found out right away." (p. 120).
8385a3127ece: <0>Falling short in daily life.</0> In Chapter 7: "Of course, we all fall much below this standard many times. But we must try to repair the damage immediately lest we pay the penalty by a spree." (p. 99).
996749edea9a: <0>At work.</0> "In case he does stumble, even once, you will have to decide whether to let him go." (p. 147). If you are sure he doesn't mean business, discharge him; if you are sure he is doing his utmost, "you may wish to give him another chance" (p. 147). A man still trying to recover who does get drunk "will tell you about it even if it means the loss of his job" (p. 146).
10e81c2700ea: So "by no means a bad thing in some cases" is as far as the program text goes. It says that, and it says no relapse is "infinitely better." It never says relapse is needed, normal, or a stage everyone goes through.
14a110fde2aa: The Foreword to the Second Edition: of alcoholics who came to A.A. and really tried, "50% got sober at once and remained that way; 25% sobered up after some relapses" (p. xx), and among the rest, those who stayed showed improvement (p. xx). That is 1955, after Dr. Bob's death.

cfc4af6fd634: Do I have to be religious to work the Steps?
2e3947cc5f62: No. You don't have to belong to a religion or accept anyone else's idea of God. The Big Book says "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47), and about half the first members thought they were atheists or agnostics (p. 44).
22cbcf4c1a4b: What the book does ask for is a willingness to believe in a Power greater than yourself. It calls this the starting point, and says that is enough to begin (p. 47).
b70fb8452918: The book is open that it is a spiritual book and that it talks about God (p. 45). Five of the Twelve Steps name God or Him. It doesn't pretend otherwise; it leaves the meaning of the word to you.
5581d611000d: What the book asks for at the start
51f4ae3f7047: Chapter 4 (pp. 44–57), "We Agnostics," was written for the reader this question is about. Its main points, in order: - Something like half the original fellowship "thought we were atheists or agnostics" (p. 44). - The book is "spiritual as well as moral," and so "we are going to talk about God" (p. 45). Here the writers expect the agnostic's face to fall, and say they've shared his doubt; some of them had been "violently anti-religious" (p. 45). - They found they "did not need to consider another's conception of God" (p. 46). Their own conception, however inadequate, was enough to begin. - "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47). - The one question needed at the start: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47) Someone who can say yes to that is "on his way" (p. 47). - How each member conceives of that Power varies widely in the stories, and these "are questions for each individual to settle for himself" (p. 50).
06476020d9a6: Where the book is not neutral
a391a7bc4030: To be fair to the text, Chapter 4 isn't indifferent about God. It argues, at length, that faith is more reasonable than unbelief (pp. 48–55). It puts the choice starkly: "either God is everything or else He is nothing" (p. 53). It asks agnostics to "lay aside prejudice, even against organized religion" (p. 49), and it ends with the story of a man who thought he was an atheist and came to "conscious companionship with his Creator" (p. 56).
24a5e3764b3d: So the book hopes the reader will come to a faith of his own. What it doesn't do is require any religion, church, creed or particular conception of God to start, or to work the Steps.
47f37e4b965f: Appendix II, written after the first printing (p. 567), says the "spiritual experience" or "spiritual awakening" the book talks about is a personality change, and that most of these develop slowly (p. 567). Interestingly, it uses "religious experiences" as another name for the same personality changes (p. 567). It then says any alcoholic can recover "provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568), and that "no one need have difficulty with the spirituality of the program" (p. 568). Willingness, honesty and open-mindedness are what's essential (p. 568).

73f7888ae869: Where is "resentment is the number one offender," and what does it mean?
47942f7acdca: It's on page 64 of Chapter 5, at the start of the Fourth Step inventory: "Resentment is the 'number one' offender." (p. 64) (The quotation marks around "number one" are the book's own.) The next sentence says why: "It destroys more alcoholics than anything else." (p. 64)

20f3d7ace7e7: It also shows where the inventory goes next: from what others did to us, to "our own mistakes" (p. 67).
197a763e3a65: Chapter 5 has just explained Step Three and the decision to turn our will and life over to God. 5709baa4fcbd: Who said "restless, irritable and discontented," and about what?
6a1a09b082bf: The words are Dr. William D. Silkworth's, not Bill W.'s. They're in his statement in "The Doctor's Opinion" at the front of the Big Book (p. xxviii), kept as he wrote it in 1939 (p. xi).
d6351b93de2e: He uses them about the drinker between drinks: "They are restless, irritable and discontented, unless they can again experience" (p. xxviii) "the sense of ease and comfort which comes at once by taking a few drinks" (p. xxix). The sentence before gives the reason men drink: "Men and women drink essentially because they like the effect produced by alcohol." (p. xxviii)
71ec16ece7b2: What follows is a cycle: they give in again, the craving develops, a spree, remorse, a firm resolution, and "This is repeated over and over" (p. xxix), with very little hope "unless this person can experience an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).
f54a0f3f6085: The printed word is "discontented," not "discontent." The context confirms the usual sense of the phrase, the alcoholic's state without a drink. It complicates one common use: Silkworth is describing drinkers caught in the cycle, not members in recovery. A member's story later in the book uses the phrase about her own sobriety (p. 317), an example of how members have come to apply it to sober life.
48c0fa5d6ca5: "The Doctor's Opinion" has three voices: A.A. members introducing the doctor, Silkworth's short letter, and his longer statement (pp. xxv–xxxii). This sentence is in the longer statement, which he signs at the end (p. xxxii). See <0>What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?</0> for the whole section.
136cd8dd74a1: The paragraph explains why the alcoholic keeps going back: 1. <0>The reason.</0> "Men and women drink essentially because they like the effect produced by alcohol." (p. xxviii) 2. <1>The confusion.</1> "The sensation is so elusive that, while they admit it is injurious, they cannot after a time differentiate the true from the false." (p. xxviii) "To them, their alcoholic life seems the only normal one." (p. xxviii) 3. <2>The state without a drink.</2> Restless, irritable and discontented, until they can feel again the ease and comfort a few drinks bring, drinks they see others take "with impunity" (p. xxix). 4. <3>The cycle.</3> They give in again, as so many do; the phenomenon of craving develops; they go through the stages of a spree and come out remorseful, "with a firm resolution not to drink again" (p. xxix). Then it repeats. 5. <4>The only way out he sees.</4> An entire psychic change (p. xxix). Once that happens, the same person who seemed doomed finds he can control his desire for alcohol, "the only effort necessary being that required to follow a few simple rules" (p. xxix).
faaa055a077b: So the restlessness is the doorway back to the drink. It sits between the sprees, in a person for whom drinking seems normal, and in the doctor's account it leads back to the drink after each firm resolution.
83d6d92f39c9: How the phrase is used in the stories
0ceea83eec12: In "My Chance to Live," a member's story in Part II of the fourth edition, the writer uses it about her own sober life: "When I am unwilling to do the right thing, I become restless, irritable, and discontent." 3062e63d35d8: The Doctor's Opinion itself doesn't say whether a sober member can feel this way. It ties the feeling to the pull back toward a drink, and its answer is the psychic change.
8799b750a246: It confirms the core of it and complicates the rest. The phrase does describe the alcoholic without a drink. 0ec064f36fea: What is the Right of Appeal, and why does the minority matter?
ccbccaca4ba2: The Right of Appeal is Bill W.'s Fifth Concept (1962): throughout A.A.'s world service structure, "minority opinion will be heard and personal grievances receive careful consideration" (p. 574).
b5459f0fb19e: It has two parts. A minority that thinks the majority is badly wrong is encouraged to file a minority report, and on a grave issue has a duty to take it to the General Service Conference. And anyone working in the structure, paid or unpaid, may petition the General Service Board over a personal grievance "without prejudice or fear of reprisal" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
9921af8a4655: Why: minorities are often right, and even when they're wrong they force a real debate. "The well-heard minority, therefore, is our chief protection against an uninformed, misinformed, hasty or angry majority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
3a451ac99a5e: A related idea is older than the Concepts. In 1946, writing about who should pay for clubs, Bill said that "the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority" (P-17, Money, 1946).
89a9dc477c76: The Long Form of the Traditions protects the individual first: A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover," and membership should never depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).
c0ecb6382310: Bill's 1946 essay on money applies it to a disagreement. Most members liked clubs, but not all, so club support should come from those who wanted them: "But the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority into supporting clubs they do not want or need" (P-17, Money, 1946).
bdb928cf0aa3: His 1947 essay on government lists among A.A.'s freedoms "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).
2065005e0c34: The 1955 Conference Charter built minority protection into elections: delegates are chosen "by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955).
6b4bbef97bf1: <0>Appeal.</0> All minorities, "whether in our staffs, committees, corporate boards or among the Trustees," should be encouraged to file minority reports when they think the majority is in considerable error (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Where a wrong decision could seriously affect A.A. as a whole, the minority should treat presenting a report to the Conference as an actual duty.
de423c61d9b1: <0>Why minorities matter.</0> "In granting this traditional ‘Right of Appeal,’ we recognize that minorities frequently can be right" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Even when partly or wholly wrong, they compel a thorough debate.
8ff760f94a6a: <0>Petition.</0> Any person in the structure may carry a personal grievance directly to the General Service Board. Bill expected it to be used seldom, but "its very existence will always tend to restrain those in authority from unjust uses of their power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
7fab1d4d3617: <0>Where it comes from.</0> Bill ties it to A.A.'s membership freedoms: "any alcoholic is a member of A.A. the moment he says so; we cannot take away his right to belong" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). "Neither can we force our members to believe anything or pay anything" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
e80a12d65c23: <0>How it already worked in 1962.</0> - <1>Electing delegates.</1> Unless a candidate gets two-thirds of the assembly, his name goes in a hat with the minority's choices, and the delegate is drawn by lot. Bill admits this sometimes sets aside the simple-majority rule, and says it has strengthened the spirit of democracy: no discontented minority trails behind the winner. - <2>The Conference's own habit.</2> "Unless it has been absolutely unavoidable, the Conference has usually refused to take important decisions on anything less than a two-thirds vote" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). - <3>The trustees' check.</3> Under the Charter, a Conference vote binds the trustees only at two-thirds of a quorum, so a narrow majority can't force them; they can insist on more debate.
b64a7e7426a7: Bill closes with Alexis de Tocqueville's warning against the "tyranny" of apathetic, self-seeking, uninformed or angry majorities, and adds the opposite danger: "the even worse tyranny of very small minorities invested with absolute power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
d8857d17f7f5: The limit: a minority can't block everything
c5c37d5077bf: Concept XII's Fourth Warranty asks for decisions by "substantial unanimity" whenever possible, but sets a limit. In a real emergency, or when "a small minority obstinately tries to use the principle of substantial unanimity to block a clearly needed action," Bill writes, "it would be the plain duty of the majority to override such a misuse of the principle of substantial unanimity" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). The Right of Appeal guarantees a hearing, not a veto.
218cd5804863: How it's done now (later sources, dated)
1e74e710a322: P-8 (first printed 1986; © 2017) describes the current Conference: after a vote reaches substantial unanimity, "those opposed are polled individually to see if they wish to speak further to their minority view" (P-8), and the Conference has sometimes reversed itself.
e2d828e43118: The 2024–2026 Service Manual: "After each vote on a matter of policy, the side that did not prevail will always be given an opportunity to speak to their position" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 6).
9048015e766a: In 1962 Bill hoped A.A. would "one day inscribe these traditional Rights" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V) in the Conference Charter. The current Charter now says the Conference recognizes "the Rights of Petition and Appeal reflected in Concepts IV and V" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Current Conference Charter) and may hear Concept V appeals from members below the Conference level. Our copy doesn't say when this was added.
c570d68c3122: Concept V was written for the world service structure: staffs, committees, boards, trustees, the Conference. It doesn't set out a procedure for a member who disagrees with a home group's decision. Bill's introduction says these principles "can of course be used to good effect throughout our entire structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), and P-8 says the same principle should apply to area committees and boards, but neither lays down rules for a group.

The word "serenity" does appear in the main text, in other senses: Bill's peace and serenity after his experience at Towns Hospital (p. 14), the hope "to match calamity with serenity" (p. 68), and the promise "We will comprehend the word serenity and we will know peace" (p. 84). None of these is the prayer.
d8a22f0f06b4: How it came into A.A.: Bill's account (1957)
77cd4a4bd856: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, Bill says that just before Ruth Hock, the office secretary, left in early 1942, "newsman Jack," a New York member, showed them a clipping (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It was an obituary notice, and under it were the words: "God grant us the serenity to accept the things we cannot change, courage to change the things we can, and wisdom to know the difference." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
986a2aa96779: "Never had we seen so much A.A. in so few words." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). A friend, Howard, came into the office and offered to pay for printing it on cards to go into every piece of mail (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). They did that for several years, and the prayer quickly came into general use, alongside "our two other favorites, the Lord's Prayer and the Prayer of St. Francis" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
272cabe6796d: On who wrote it, Bill says some credited the early Greeks, some an anonymous English poet, some an American naval officer, and that Jack Alexander, who had looked into it, "attributes it to the Rev. Reinhold Niebuhr of the Union Theological Seminary" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill's conclusion: "Anyhow, we have the prayer and it is said thousands of times daily." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
452226aba42d: The later biography gives more detail. It says the prayer was found in the "In Memoriam" column of an early June 1941 edition of the New York Herald-Tribune (Pass It On, 1984). It gives the notice's wording, addressed to "Mother" and beginning "Mother — God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change" (Pass It On, 1984), going on with "I can" in the second line and ending "Goodbye."
733c2ee52855: It quotes Ruth Hock: "Jack C. appeared at the office one morning, and he showed me the obituary notice" (Pass It On, 1984), and she copied it to use in letters to groups and loners. In her account, "Horace C. had the idea of printing it on cards and paid for the first printing" (Pass It On, 1984). Elsewhere <0>Pass It On</0> notes that in his 1957 book Bill called Horace C. "Howard A." (Pass It On, 1984), so the two accounts may name the same man.
544b95e6341b: A note in <0>Pass It On</0> says the prayer's origins are obscure: it may go back to the philosopher Boethius, about 500 A.D.; it is usually credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, a 20th-century theologian, who in turn credited an 18th-century theologian (Pass It On, 1984). Our copy of that note is damaged by the scan, so the second theologian's name can't be read with confidence.
c6ef7348b0fe: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> quotes an early Ohio member, Oscar W., describing the friction between the Midwest and New York in the 1940s: "I don't like the Serenity Prayer. New York brought it in, and we resented it." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). To him it felt like the Oxford Group's praying coming back.
1d610b0679ea: Later A.A. literature describes the prayer as a common part of meetings. P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> (© 2018), describing how a chairperson usually opens a meeting with the Preamble, adds: "Some call for a moment of silence and/or recite the Serenity Prayer" (P-16). In one fourth-edition story, a member describes the slogans on a meeting-room wall, ending with "The Serenity Prayer" (p. 345). Another says he had misread "the courage to change" as being about changing his marriage, when it meant changing himself (p. 419).
2430c68e69ba: <0>When.</0> Bill (1957) puts it just before Ruth Hock left in early 1942 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says an early June 1941 newspaper (Pass It On, 1984).
08bf1ca240ab: <0>The wording.</0> Bill's version reads "grant us… we cannot change… we can" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); <1>Pass It On</1> gives the clipping as "grant me… I cannot change… I can" (Pass It On, 1984). The fourth-edition stories that quote it use the "us… we" form (pp. 357, 559).
7387e03ceca8: <0>Who paid for the cards.</0> "Friend Howard" in 1957 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); Horace C. in Ruth Hock's memory, 1984 (Pass It On, 1984).
bdb4caa2ae06: <0>Who wrote it.</0> Bill (1957) says no one can be sure (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) calls the origins obscure (Pass It On, 1984). Both mention Niebuhr as the usual attribution; neither settles it, and neither does our sources.

5e353acd3ba7: What is the Seventh Step prayer, and where is it?
802d4a9ed473: It's on page 76 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action." It begins "My Creator, I am now willing that you should have all of me, good and bad." (p. 76)
98a0cc0a7071: The book introduces it with "When ready, we say something like this" (p. 76). So it's an example, not a set form, and the book doesn't call it "the Seventh Step prayer."
2239597effde: It asks for defects to be removed for a reason outside yourself: because they stand in the way of "my usefulness to you and my fellows" (p. 76).
8137df30c280: Steps Six and Seven read: "Were entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character." and "Humbly asked Him to remove our shortcomings." (p. 59)
e003c3befe52: In Chapter 6 they come right after the Fifth Step. Having told someone their whole story, members go home, find a quiet hour, and reread the first five Steps to check nothing has been left out (p. 75). Then the book turns to Step Six, and the whole of Steps Six and Seven takes one paragraph each (p. 76).
6b91bf774390: Step Six, in the book's words
2c6fa4b73daf: Step Six is about willingness, which the book has "emphasized" as "indispensable" (p. 76). The question is whether we're ready to let God remove all the things we've admitted are objectionable: "Can He now take them all—every one?" (p. 76) If we still cling to something, "we ask God to help us be willing" (p. 76).
a610502be460: "When ready" (p. 76), the book gives the prayer. After its opening line, it asks God to remove "every single defect of character" that stands in the way of usefulness to God and to other people, and asks for strength to do God's bidding "as I go out from here" (p. 76). Then: "We have then completed Step Seven." (p. 76)
